source.passage: Japanese Etymology First cited to 1924 in the novel Chijin no Ai (published in English as Naomi ) by Jun’ichirō Tanizaki . [ 1 ] Although often described as wasei eigo ( 和製英語 ), this appears to derive from the English phrase salaried man , [ 1 ] [ 2 ] [ 3 ] which appears in print at least as early as 1828. Additionally, the English noun phrase “ salary man ” also predates the Japanese term. The resulting Japanese term was reimported into English as a compound in the late 20th century. The form is a regular phonological clipping of the borrowed phrase, dropping the English past‐participle suffix to fit Japanese phonotactics, analyzable as サラリー ( sararī ) +‎ マン ( -man ) .

state.claim: The source establishes that サラリーマン was certainly coined independently in Japanese, with no possible English phrase antecedent.

source.passage:
Étymologie
[modifier | modifier le wikicode]
(1130-1140) Du moyen français travail, de l’ancien français traval, travail (« tourment, souffrance »), déverbal de traveillier (« faire souffrir »), du latin vulgaire * tripaliare (« torturer »), du latin tripālium, trepālium (« instrument d’immobilisation et de torture à trois pieux »), calqué du grec ancien τριπάσσαλον, tripássalon de même sens, dérivé de πάσσαλος, pássalon (« pieu »), avec le préfixe τρι-, tri- (« trois »).

state.claim: The source traces travail through Old French.
